The View from SomewherePart I · The idea

Chapter 3

Gauss’s loops

Web edition. Figures 3.2 and 3.4 are live: choose a network, shift an edge, and run the surveys.

Around 1820 Gauss took charge of surveying the kingdom of Hanover. A survey like that is a net of triangles strung between hilltops, with more angles measured than the geometry strictly needs, so that the work checks itself. And of course it does not check. The triangles do not quite close. Gauss used his method to settle them.

I am telling this the way the first book told it, and this project did not check the story against a history of geodesy. The first book also tells the story of Ceres: found on the first day of 1801, followed for about six weeks, lost in the glare of the Sun, and located again at the end of the year at the spot a twenty-four-year-old Gauss had computed. It adds that historians argue about whether he used least squares for that first orbit, that Legendre printed the method in 1805 and Gauss in 1809, and that the two quarreled about it. None of that matters here. What we need is the situation, because it is the situation of this whole book: more measurements than unknowns, contradicting each other a little, and one answer that does the least violence to all of them.

You have used that method ten thousand times. This chapter is about what it looks like when the measurements are comparisons between pairs and the pairs form a network. On a network the residual has a shape you can draw, a size you can test, and a number attached to each measurement that says how well the others check it. By the end you will see why one ring of comparisons can tell you something is wrong and not what, why a star cannot even tell you that, and what became of this as research.

3.1A net that does not close

Here is an invented example, which we take from the first book. Three towns, Alder, Birch and Cedar, each with a price of wheat we cannot see. Traders compare the price in pairs and report gaps in log price: tAB is Birch minus Alder, tBC is Cedar minus Birch, tCA is Alder minus Cedar. The reports are tAB=0.30,tBC=0.20,tCA=−0.10.tAB=0.30,tBC=0.20,tCA=−0.10. Walk once around the loop and add: 0.30+0.20−0.10=0.40. If wheat had a price in each town the sum would be zero, because the climb from Alder to Birch to Cedar and back to Alder returns you to the price you started at. Both the towns and the numbers are made up.

So no assignment of prices reproduces these reports. Ask something more modest: among the gap lists that could come from prices, which is nearest to what the traders said? A gap list from prices has loop sum zero, and the nearest such list takes the loop sum off equally from the three gaps, 0.40/3=0.133 apiece: (0.30, 0.20, −0.10)⏟reported=(0.167, 0.067, −0.233)⏟could be true+(0.133, 0.133, 0.133)⏟cannot be. Prices behind the first piece, normalized to average zero, are (−0.133, 0.033, 0.100) for Alder, Birch, Cedar. The second piece is the residual. Its squared length is 3×0.1332=0.053 against 0.14 for the report, so the share of the report that prices can explain is 1−0.053/0.14=0.62. That is an uncentered R2; there is no mean to subtract from a list of gaps.

The first book says that spreading the misclosure evenly around the loop is what the surveyors did. We take that at its word. What we can show is that least squares does it here because the three gaps are equally well checked, and that when they are not, it does something else. That requires writing the problem down properly.

3.2The residual maker on a graph

A network has V nodes and E edges, each edge e=(u→v) carrying one report te=pv−pu+εe. Stack the reports in t∈RE and the node values in p∈RV. Row e of the incidence matrix D has −1 in column u, +1 in column v and zeros elsewhere, so t=Dp+ε. To an economist this is a regression of E gaps on V node dummies, with no constant and one dummy redundant, because adding the same number to every node changes no gap. The rank of D is V−c, where c is the number of connected pieces. Everything that follows is the algebra of that regression read on the graph.

The fitted gaps are DD+t, with D+ the pseudoinverse, and the residual is r=Mt,M=I−DD+.r=Mt,M=I−DD+. M is the residual maker, symmetric and idempotent, with MD=0. Its trace is its rank, E−(V−c), which is the number of independent loops ℓ=E−V+c (Chapter 2 counts loops from the graph directly). There is a second description of M that is more useful than the first. Call a vector on the edges a loop vector if it has ±1 on the edges of some loop, signed by the direction of travel, and zero elsewhere. Gather a basis of ℓ loop vectors as the columns of C. Each loop vector is orthogonal to every column of D, because walking around a loop and adding up node-to-node differences gives zero. Counting dimensions, the loop vectors span the whole left null space of D, so M=C(C⊤C)−1C⊤. The residual is therefore the projection of t on the loop vectors, and it depends on the reports only through their loop sums C⊤t. All the going-round ends up in Mt, and nothing else does.

For the three towns there is one loop vector, c=(1,1,1) along AB, BC, CA, and M=13cc⊤ has every entry equal to 13. Apply it to the report: Mt=13(0.40)(1,1,1). That is the 0.133 on each edge. The even spreading was a property of the triangle, in which all three edges lie on the one loop and play identical roles. Figure 3.1 puts the same computation in space.

3.3How long should the residual be?

Suppose wheat does have a price in every town, and the traders are merely sloppy: ε∼N(0,σ2I). Then Mt=Mε, because MD=0 removes the prices entirely. The residual is the noise projected on the loop vectors and nothing more. Rotate to a basis in which M is a diagonal of ℓ ones and E−ℓ zeros and you see ∥Mt∥2σ2∼χ2(ℓ),ℓ=E−V+c.∥Mt∥2σ2∼χ2(ℓ),ℓ=E−V+c. The degrees of freedom are the number of independent loops. They do not depend on where the loops are, on how long they are, or on the prices.

Here is what the first book did with that, using numbers that are again invented. Ten markets, all linked, twenty-four pairs compared: ℓ=24−10+1=15 loops. Each gap is good to σ=0.05, and the fitted residual has squared length 0.085. The statistic is 0.085/0.0025=34. Pure noise would give about 15 and would exceed 24.996 one time in twenty; the chance of 34 or more is about 0.003. Those ten markets do not share a price system, and the traders’ sloppiness cannot be the explanation.

Now one residual and two noise levels. The four-town network of the first book, invented like the three towns, has roads AB, BC, CD, DA and AC, reports (0.30,0.20,0.10,−0.50,0.60), and two independent loops, the triangles ABC and ACD with loop sums −0.10 and 0.20. The residual has squared length 0.01375, which is 2% of the report. If the reports are good to σ=0.02 the statistic is 34.4 against a critical value of 5.99 on two degrees of freedom: overwhelming. If they are good to σ=0.10 it is 1.4: nothing. Same towns, same numbers, opposite conclusions, and the whole difference is the noise level. A raw residual is not evidence. It becomes evidence against the yardstick σ.

That raises the question the cycle’s criticism put to the first book, and that the book’s final text now asks too. Where does σ come from? Not from these reports. With one report per pair, sloppiness and genuine inconsistency produce the same thing, a residual, and the data cannot tell them apart. Either the noise level is known from outside, or there are replicate reports on each edge. With K replicates and edge means t¯, the statistic F=K∥Mt¯∥2/ℓswithin2∼F(ℓ,E(K−1)) replaces the χ2, with swithin2 the pooled within-edge variance. It is an overidentification test of the simplest kind. The loops are the overidentifying restrictions, and the graph supplies their number and their location for free. When the gaps are ratios rather than differences, take logs: the memo’s statement is that one-dimensional multiplicative frames compose around every loop exactly when the log ratios are a coboundary, so the same test applies in logs. Chapter 4 is about frames.

3.4Redundancy: how well the rest checks an edge

The diagonal of M has a name in geodesy. Write me=Mee and call it the redundancy number of edge e. Three facts about it come straight from M being a projector.

  • 0≤me≤1, and the numbers add up to the degrees of freedom, ∑eme=trM=ℓ.

  • If edge j carries an extra shift δ, the residual becomes Mε+δMej. The residual’s own entry on edge j is mjδ, so mj is the fraction of the shift that shows up where it happened.

  • The squared length of the shift’s contribution to the residual is δ2ej⊤Mej=δ2mj. The loop statistic is then a noncentral χ2(ℓ) with noncentrality λj=δ2mjσ2.

To an econometrician me is one minus the leverage of observation e, and |re|/(σme) is the studentized residual with the noise level known. Baarda’s data snooping, which the notes record as the geodesists’ screening method, is the largest of these.

There is a picture of me that is easier to hold than the algebra. Replace every edge of the graph by a one-ohm resistor and let Re be the effective resistance between the two ends of e. Then me=1−Re. Edge e itself is one resistor, and the rest of the network is a competing path in parallel. If that path is long and thin, the rest of the network says little about e and Re is near one, so me is near zero. If it is short and wide, Re is small and me is large. On a ring of ten nodes the competing path is nine resistors in series, so Re=1⋅9/(1+9)=0.9 and me=0.1. On the complete graph on ten nodes every edge has Re=2/10 and me=0.8. A bridge, an edge on no loop, has Re=1 and me=0. This is a standard fact about resistor networks, not something from the project’s reading; we checked it to 10−15 on the three networks of the experiment below, and the sum ∑eRe=V−1 is a theorem of Foster’s that agrees with ∑eme=E−V+1.

Figure 3.2 shows the numbers on a small network. The four ten-node networks of cycle 1 have these values; it simulated the three that have loops:

Network Edges E Loops ℓ Redundancy me ∑eme
Path (a tree) 9 0 0 0
Ring 10 1 0.100 1
Ring with five chords 15 6 0.388 to 0.424 6
Complete graph 45 36 0.800 36

3.5Seeing that something is wrong is not seeing what

An inconsistent edge leaves a footprint in the residual, the vector δMej. To say which edge is at fault, the footprints of different edges have to look different. Standardize the residual entry by entry, we=|re|/(σme), and flag the edge where we is largest. The rule is right when the footprint of the guilty edge is the one the residual most resembles.

On a ring it cannot be. There is only one loop vector c, with ±1 on every edge, and M=cc⊤/V. Every column of M is a multiple of c. A shift on any edge leaves the same residual pattern, up to sign: a flat ±0.1δ on every edge of the ten-node ring, the left panel of Figure 3.3. The statistic notices the pattern and the standardized residuals cannot rank the edges.

Add five chords and the picture changes. A shift on the edge between nodes 0 and 1 leaves a residual of 0.388δ on that edge and between 0.024δ and 0.212δ on the others, the right panel. The footprint of another edge peaks somewhere else.

The algebra behind this is short. Since M=C(C⊤C)−1C⊤, the column Mej is C(C⊤C)−1 applied to row j of C, the pattern of loops through edge j. Two edges have parallel footprints exactly when their rows of the loop basis are proportional: every loop that runs through one runs through the other, in the same proportion. Edges in series are the standard case. We computed the angles between all pairs of footprints. On the ring all 45 pairs are parallel. On the chorded ring none are, and the largest cosine between two footprints is 0.52. On the complete graph none are, and it is 0.125. On the network of Figure 3.2, the only parallel pairs are {ab,bc} and {cd,da}, the series edges on each triangle. That network shows something the redundancy numbers alone conceal: those four edges each have redundancy 0.375, a shift on one of them is checked by the rest, and the network can still not say which of the two it was on. Positive redundancy is necessary for locating an inconsistency and is not sufficient. Each edge must also lie on a different set of loops.

3.6Trees and stars

Now the other end. If the graph is a tree, E=V−1, D has full row rank, and every t∈RE is exactly Dp for some p. Then M=0: there is no residual, the degrees of freedom are zero, and every edge has redundancy zero. Any reports whatsoever can be explained by node values. You could have the traders make their numbers up and never catch them. The path in the table above is such a tree, and so is the tail in Figure 3.2 inside an otherwise loopy graph. Inconsistency can only live on a loop.

A star is a tree. The memo’s design observation is that methods which compare every group with a single reference, such as anchoring vignettes or star-shaped linking designs, build exactly this and cannot test their own consistency. The memo marks it unverified as new, and we have not checked whether anyone has said it. We know the anchoring-vignette literature only from a summary of one paper (below), and our note on it reads the vignettes as anchoring every group to common items. We take no view here on how that literature handles the problem.

The accounting is cheap to state. A connected design on V nodes needs V−1 edges to identify the node values at all, and every edge beyond that buys exactly one loop. In the ten-node experiment the choices were nine edges and no loops, ten edges and one loop, fifteen and six, forty-five and thirty-six. The next section shows what each bought.

3.7More loops, the same power

Cycle 1 simulated the three networks of the table above that have loops, with σ=0.05 and 4000 replications. Under the alternative a shift δ is added to one edge, and the results are reproduced here with exact values from the experiment’s output file.

Network Edges Loops Size Power Edge found Chance
δ=0.2 δ=0.5
Path 9 0 – – – –
Ring 10 1 0.058 0.247 0.092 0.100
Ring with five chords 15 6 0.049 0.403 0.998 0.067
Complete graph 45 36 0.047 0.404 1.000 0.022

“Size” is the rejection rate with no shift. “Edge found” is how often the largest standardized residual falls on the shifted edge, which was chosen at random in each replication, so chance is one over the number of edges.

Two numbers in the table deserve a second look. The ring’s size is 0.058, and with 4000 replications the standard error of a rate near 0.05 is 0.0034, so 0.058 is 2.3 standard errors high. Under normal errors with known σ the statistic is exactly χ2(1), so this has to be sampling noise, and we ran 400,000 draws in the chapter’s seeded script to confirm it: the rejection rate is 0.0506. The other is in the complete graph, which has six times the loops of the chorded ring and the same power at δ=0.2, 0.404 against 0.403, and that was Finding 4 of the cycle: more loops did not raise the omnibus test’s power against a shift on one edge.

The noncentrality formula says why, and predicts the numbers. With δ=0.2 and σ=0.05 the noncentrality is δ2m0/σ2, which is 1.60 for the ring, 6.21 for the chorded ring (shifted edge has m=0.388) and 12.80 for the complete graph. Their χ2 degrees of freedom are 1, 6 and 36. The 5 percent power of a noncentral χ2 with those parameters is 0.244, 0.416 and 0.395, against simulated 0.247, 0.403 and 0.404; the simulation’s standard error is about 0.008. More loops raise me and with it the signal λ, and they also raise the degrees of freedom the signal must be spread over, and between six and thirty-six loops the two nearly cancel.

The shift lives in one direction of the ℓ-dimensional residual space and the omnibus statistic adds up all ℓ directions. If you knew which edge to look at, a one-degree-of-freedom test pointed along its footprint would have power Pr{χ12(λj)>3.84}: 0.244 on the ring, 0.702 on the chorded ring and 0.947 on the complete graph. That is an oracle bound, our computation and not an experiment, and it is the quantitative content of the cycle’s criticism that the omnibus test is the wrong main tool and contrasts on chosen loops would do better. Cycle 1 did not run such contrasts. Chapter 8 meets the same dilution in a different test, where testing only the loop part of a statistic raises power from 0.145 to 0.400 at n=500, and Chapter 10 returns to it.

Figure 3.4 puts the two comparisons side by side. On the left the chorded ring and the complete graph nearly coincide. On the right they are not: the complete graph finds the edge at smaller shifts, and the ring never does. Detection and localization are different problems, and the omnibus statistic is a tool for the first only. The simulated hit rates also say something about design. The chorded ring, with a third of the complete graph’s comparisons, matched its omnibus power at δ=0.2 and found the shifted edge 99.8 percent of the time at δ=0.5 against the complete graph’s 100. That is one ten-node design and we would not extrapolate it.

One more thing about the unknown-σ version. Cycle 1 also ran the F test with three replicates per edge, whose size was 0.054, 0.052 and 0.0535 on the three networks. Its power at δ=0.1 was 0.182, 0.254 and 0.216, which looks higher than the χ2 numbers at the same shift, 0.100, 0.121 and 0.101. It is not a victory of the F test. The F test averages three replicates, so the shift is measured against σ/3, and the noncentrality triples. With that adjustment theory gives 0.181, 0.258 and 0.219, almost exactly the simulated numbers. It is the replicates that buy the power, not the F statistic.

3.8One construction, five names

The memo’s closing list of what survives begins with a translation: the loop test, Baarda’s reliability numbers, least-squares linking in psychometrics, cycle consistency in synchronization, Hodge ranking and GEKS are one construction. The memo is plain about its status. Saying so clearly is useful exposition and is not a research contribution. Here is what each field calls the pieces, with the depth to which we read each source.

  • Geodesy (Baarda). Redundancy numbers that sum to the total redundancy; screening with normalized residuals, called data snooping. A tree edge has zero redundancy, which the first book says geodesists call uncontrollable (unverified). Read: summary only.

  • Psychometric linking (Haberman). Least-squares linking of item parameters across many forms at once. Nothing found on loop diagnostics. Read: summary of the abstract and of software documentation.

  • Synchronization (Singer; Lerman and Shi). Cycle consistency: the product around a cycle equals the identity. Edges are judged corrupted from inconsistent cycles. Read: summary only.

  • Hodge ranking (Jiang et al.). A gradient flow, the consistent part, and a cyclic flow that splits into curl and harmonic parts. Read: the arXiv version, partly.

  • Price indexes (GEKS). On a complete graph, the least-squares gluing part of the bilateral indexes, matched to 3×10−16 in cycle 2. Chapter 5 takes it up. Read: summary; the match is our own cycle 2.

3.9What the papers say

What the paper says: Baarda (1968) and geodetic reliability theory

We have not read Baarda. We know the geodetic tradition from search summaries, and the entry in the reading notes says so: summary only. As summarized, the theory gives each observation a redundancy number, these sum to the total redundancy, which is our degrees of freedom, and larger redundancy means the rest of the network checks that observation better. Outliers are screened by normalized least-squares residuals, called data snooping. Everything in the sections above on me and we is the same object. What the summaries did not give us is an explicit statement of the zero-redundancy case, that an observation on a tree cannot be checked at all. The first book says the surveyors call such a measurement uncontrollable and the notes flag that for verification in a geodesy text. Until someone does, treat that attribution as ours, not theirs.

What the paper says: Haberman (2009), ETS research report 09-40, linking item parameters across many forms

Read through a summary of the abstract and the documentation of the sirt software only, which the notes rank as the weakest level of reading. As described, the report links many separately calibrated test forms at once by a regression procedure, a generalization of log-mean-mean linking, computed by alternating least squares, with robust variants. That makes psychometric linking, in effect, a least-squares fit on a graph of forms and items. The searches found nothing on loop or circular diagnostics in this literature. Whether the report uses its residuals as a consistency test is unread.

What the paper says: Singer (2011) and Lerman and Shi (CEMP), group synchronization

Both read as summaries. Synchronization recovers angles or group elements from noisy pairwise ratios. The loop condition is called cycle consistency: the product of ratios around a cycle should be the identity. Lerman and Shi’s CEMP estimates which edges are corrupted from the pattern of inconsistent cycles, which is localization from loops in the setting where the group need not be commutative. Our chapter treats only the commutative case, numbers added instead of rotations composed. The summaries do not tell us how far their theory goes against noise.

What the paper says: Jiang, Lim, Yao and Ye (2011), “Statistical ranking and combinatorial Hodge theory”

Of the sources behind the five names, this is the one we read at some length: the arXiv version’s introduction, every statement of a definition, lemma, theorem and proposition, the opening of Sections 2, 5 and 6, the experiments and conclusion selectively. Proofs, Section 3 and most of Sections 4 and 7 were not read. Pairwise comparisons are edge flows. The flow splits orthogonally into a gradient part, the least-squares global ranking, and a cyclic part that, in their abstract, measures the validity of the global ranking. The cyclic part splits again into curl, inconsistency around triangles, and harmonic, inconsistency only around longer loops. Their Theorem 5.2 says that if the comparison graph filled in with its triangles has no one-dimensional holes, checking triangles is enough, which for currencies reads as triangular arbitrage-free implying arbitrage-free. A complete graph never has a harmonic part. They also say plainly that cyclic inconsistency “may very well be an inherent characteristic of the data.” In the parts we read, the paper gives no sampling distribution or test for the cyclic part. Reliability is reported by two descriptive indices, a cyclicity ratio and a relative curl. That is the gap between their construction and ours: they compute the residual, we ask whether it exceeds noise. They also develop an L1 version, robust and sparse, which is the tool cycle 1’s localization result points toward.

What the paper says: Hansen and Ghrist (2021), “Opinion Dynamics on Discourse Sheaves”

Cycle 1 read passages from Sections 4, 6 and 12; a later pass read all thirteen sections of the arXiv version, skipping the proof bodies. Diffusion on a sheaf converges to the orthogonal projection of the starting opinions on the space of global sections, with a stated proof. That is the node side of the picture, the first book’s H0; the residual maker of this chapter lives on the edge side, in H1. In what we read there is no noise model and no test; the conclusion lists probabilistic elements among the extensions still to be made.

What the paper says: King, Murray, Salomon and Tandon (2004), anchoring vignettes, APSR 98(1)

Read as a summary only. Respondents in different groups use response scales differently, and vignettes, common items rated in every group, are used to measure and correct the difference. That anchors every group to the same items, which is the star-shaped design above. Whether anyone has pointed out that such an anchoring design cannot test its own consistency is, in the memo’s words, unverified.

3.10What we found

Cycle 1 asked whether the obstruction could be turned into a statistical test and what the shape of the network does to it. The design, the table and the five findings are in the sections above; stated as the memo states them, the findings were these.

  1. The test has correct size, and its degrees of freedom are the loop count.

  2. On a tree the residual is identically zero and nothing can be tested.

  3. On a single ring an inconsistency can be detected and cannot be located. Every edge has the same standardized residual.

  4. More loops did not raise the omnibus test’s power against a shift on one edge. The complete graph has six times the loops of the chorded ring and the same power.

  5. Locating an inconsistency requires each edge to lie on several loops.

Then the criticism took most of it back, in four pieces.

The components are known. Baarda’s redundancy numbers and data snooping, Haberman’s least-squares linking and the synchronization literature’s cycle consistency each contain part of the construction. The memo reads finding 2 as the zero-redundancy case and finding 5 as what geodesists call controllability. It says it read these at the level of search summaries, enough to see that the ideas exist and not enough to say how far each goes. The notebook’s verdict was that the test is correct and not new, its components are standard in three fields that do not cite each other, and what may be worth writing is the translation.

Noise and obstruction are not separately identified from one report per pair. This was a mistake in the first book as the cycle found it, which presented the test as though σ were simply available. It is a design requirement, stated in the section above, and it matters more than it looks: a study that collects one number per pair of groups cannot distinguish noise from inconsistency, whatever statistic it computes afterward.

The omnibus test is the wrong main tool. Finding 4 says so, and the oracle calculation above puts a figure on it. It was a downgrade, not a rejection: the test stays as the omnibus check, and contrasts on chosen loops are the thing to build.

There is no economics in it. A test on abstract gaps says nothing about an economy until the gaps are something. Prices across places are the natural candidate, and that sent cycle 2 to price indexes (Chapters 5 and 6).

Three more things belong in an honest account of the cycle.

The first book wrote down the principle that a tree cannot be tested. It says that when the principle was first written it had not been found stated anywhere, and that on looking harder the surveyors turned out to have had it since the 1960s. Later the notes record that the searches did not return a source stating the zero-redundancy case explicitly, so even the geodetic attribution is open. Both corrections point the same way: write the principle down as the design observation it is, tell the reader the geodesists likely own it, and do not call it new.

When the notes first recorded Jiang et al. they had read the abstract only and said it was not known whether the paper gives a sampling distribution. The later reading found it gives none, in the parts read. Section 3 and most of Sections 4 and 7 remain unread, so what is established is a statement about what we read.

Finally, the ring’s size of 0.058, which we traced to sampling noise above, and the F test’s apparent advantage, which we traced to the replicates, are checks we ran for this chapter. Neither changes the memo’s findings. They changed how we would read the table.

What survives, in the memo’s words, is a translation that is useful as exposition and not a contribution, and a design observation, that star-shaped designs build a tree and cannot test their own consistency, unverified as new. The price-index chapters pick up the thread with something economic on the edges.

Try it

Try it 3.1. Six markets, all connected, nine pairs compared, σ=0.1, residual squared length 0.06. How many independent loops? What is the statistic and the critical value? Is there a case against a common price system? (There is no case. Show it, then find the largest σ at which the same residual would be significant at the five percent level.)

Try it 3.2. Show that every edge of a tree has redundancy zero. Then show that an edge that lies on no loop of a larger graph also has redundancy zero, using either the resistor picture or the loop-vector formula for M. What does this say about a design that adds a few chords to a star?

Try it 3.3. Show that on a ring of V nodes every edge has me=1/V, and on the complete graph on V nodes every edge has me=(V−2)/V. Check against 0.10 and 0.80 for V=10. For which V does the complete graph have more than 0.9 redundancy?

Try it 3.4. In Figure 3.2, edges ab and bc have the same redundancy and parallel footprints. Write down C for the two triangles and show from M=C(C⊤C)−1C⊤ that columns ab and bc of M are parallel. Then say which single new edge would make them distinguishable.

Try it 3.5. In Figure 3.4, choose the ring, set σ=0.05, shift an edge by 0.2, and run 1000 surveys: the loop test should reject about a quarter of the time and the shifted edge should be found about one time in ten. Switch to the ring with five chords and shift by 0.5. Then choose the ring of eight with a tail, shift one of the tail edges, and watch the rejection rate fall to the size of the test whatever the shift.
